name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
title: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
answer: An institutional knowledge graph is a structured representation of the entities and relationships that matter to a research organization, such as people, publications, datasets, projects, grants, equipment, and organizational units. It connects these entities across silos so that a researcher, a librarian, or an administrator can follow a trail from a paper to its authors, funders, data, and related works. The scope is usually bounded by the institution's own records but often includes external identifiers and linked open data to place local work in a wider context. It is not a search index or a document store; it is a curated model of how institutional knowledge fits together.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: An institutional knowledge graph is a structured representation of the entities and relationships that matter to a research organization, such as people, publications, datasets, projects, grants, equipment, and organizational units. It connects these entities across silos so that a researcher, a librarian, or an administrator can follow a trail from a paper to its authors, funders, data, and related works. The scope is usually bounded by the institution's own records but often includes external identifiers and linked open data to place local work in a wider context. It is not a search index or a document store; it is a curated model of how institutional knowledge fits together.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The graph typically runs on a graph database or a triple store, with an ontology or schema defining allowed node and edge types. It draws from existing systems such as a current research information system, an institutional repository, a human resources directory, and a grants management platform. Data is often loaded through extract, transform, and load pipelines that map local fields to shared vocabularies. Query access is usually provided through a graph query language or a SPARQL endpoint, and the graph may be exposed to internal dashboards or public discovery interfaces.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Building the graph starts with ontology design, where domain experts and data stewards agree on the classes and properties that matter, for example Person, Publication, Dataset, and the relations authors, cites, and funds. Entity resolution then merges records that refer to the same real world thing, using identifiers like ORCID for people, DOI for outputs, and ROR for organizations. Extraction from unstructured text, such as abstracts or grant narratives, can add claims, but these are usually kept separate from authoritative administrative records. Curation is ongoing, with versioned updates and review workflows to correct errors and add new relationships.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on who may see, edit, and reuse the graph, because it can combine public research outputs with personal data about staff, students, and collaborators. Provenance must record where each fact came from, whether a human resources system, a publisher metadata feed, or an automated extractor, and when it was last updated. Access control is often role based, with public views limited to non personal research information and internal views carrying employment or funding details. Data protection law and institutional policy shape retention, consent, and the right to correct or remove records, so the graph needs clear ownership and a change log.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs are moving toward greater interoperability through shared ontologies and federation across institutions, so that a query can span several universities without copying all data into one place. AI assisted curation is likely to reduce the cost of entity resolution and claim extraction, but human review will remain important for trust. Graph based retrieval and embeddings may support research discovery, collaboration matching, and impact assessment. The long term direction is a living, machine readable map of institutional research activity that stays close to its sources and respects the rights of the people it describes.
